input: Consumers should be allowed to contest any portion of a credit-card debt that exceeds the balance owed when the account first went into default. Once such a dispute is raised, penalties, fees, and additional interest on the disputed amount should be frozen while the creditor and consumer work toward a fair repayment plan. This would give card issuers and debt collectors an incentive to negotiate instead of benefiting from a balance that keeps growing after default. A growing balance can make repayment less realistic even when a consumer is willing to pay. Credit card issuers can raise interest rates on delinquent accounts to levels around 29.9% under some account terms. When high interest is combined with repeated fees, the amount demanded can rise substantially after the original default. That creates an unfair dynamic in which delay can work against the debtor rather than toward repayment. I closed my Emmy award-winning regional video business so I could care for my parents, and my savings were eventually depleted. I contacted all of my credit card providers before I missed a payment to explain the situation. None of them offered useful guidance beyond telling me to make sure I paid the bill on time. I had maintained one Citibank credit-card account for 15 years without delinquency. After I defaulted, Citibank added $5,000 to the amount I had owed. I challenged that increase as excessive and explained why I had fallen behind, but neither Citibank nor the debt collector showed concern. That experience convinced me that creditors have little reason to reconsider post-default additions when consumers can only ask for cooperation. If successfully contested charges were removed and the enforceable balance returned to what was owed at default, creditors such as Citibank would have a stronger reason to work with consumers. Such a rule would not erase the original debt; consumers would remain responsible for what they owed at default, while creditors would have to justify later additions.

I propose that the CFPB adopt a rule preventing a creditor or debt collector from sending a disputed debt to a new collection agency after the consumer has contested the debt or sent a cease-and-desist letter. In cases I have managed, I sent cease-and-desist letters to both the collection agency and the original creditor. The letters invoked the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) and asked that collection efforts stop. Even after those notices, the creditor ended the current agency's assignment and placed the same debt with another collector. The consumer then had to repeat the dispute process with the new agency, turning one objection into a continuing cycle. Reassigning the account this way defeats the purpose of notice because the consumer must keep responding to new collectors about the same debt. The CFPB should require a debt collector receiving a dispute or cease-and-desist letter to notify the original creditor and preserve that status with the account. The original creditor should flag the account so it is not placed with another collector while the dispute or communication restriction remains unresolved. A durable account-level record would make the notice follow the debt when one agency is replaced. Before another transfer, the creditor should document that the dispute or notice has been resolved.

Credit card agreements are adhesion contracts drafted by issuers, leaving consumers little power to negotiate terms. Independent oversight is important when those contracts produce harsh results a borrower could not prevent. A consumer whose income collapses after a catastrophe should be allowed to pause interest, penalties, and fees until the crisis passes. The pause should apply only to documented hardship and should not erase principal already owed. A borrower who intends to repay should not be treated like someone deliberately refusing to pay. Floods, wildfires, earthquakes, and similar disasters can destroy homes, interrupt work, and eliminate payment income. Adding charges then can turn temporary inability to pay into a much larger debt. That is unfair when missed payments arise from circumstances outside the consumer's control. Credit card companies should not obscure post-default charges in dense contract language. An independent reviewer or court should decide whether a hardship qualifies and whether added charges are equitable. Once the consumer recovers, normal repayment could resume. This preserves the promise to repay without assuming payment is possible under every condition. Insurance policies often exclude acts of war. Yet the World Trade Center owner was permitted to pursue insurance recovery after 9/11 despite disputes over the attacks' characterization. I see that as an example of allowing extraordinary circumstances instead of applying contract language mechanically. Polls after the 2008 bailouts reported broad dissatisfaction that ordinary Americans received little direct relief. That history makes it troubling when institutions receive crisis flexibility while individual borrowers receive none. The credit-card 'Promise to Pay' should not require uninterrupted monthly payments under every imaginable condition. It should mean the borrower remains responsible for legitimate debt and resumes payment when reasonably able. I think judges have read that promise without enough attention to catastrophic hardship. I also believe lawyers may avoid challenging weaknesses in standard-form credit card contracts when doing so threatens established work.

When Bayview, a debt collection firm, took over servicing my mortgage, it began calling me at work and on my cell phone about the status of my payments. My mortgage payments were current, and I had not been late. Some contacts were automated calls even though there was no delinquent balance. When I asked about the calls, I was told they were routine and that I should ignore them. I found that explanation unacceptable because collection-style contacts can make a borrower feel as though an account is in default when it is not. I filed a complaint with the Better Business Bureau. I have consistently paid this mortgage on time, and our mortgage has never been placed in debt collection. Bayview also operates as a debt collection agency, but its collection activity should be kept separate from ordinary mortgage servicing. A company handling both functions should distinguish delinquent borrowers from customers whose accounts are current. Otherwise, collection practices can spill into routine servicing and pressure people who owe nothing past due. Mortgage servicers should not call a current borrower at work for routine payment-status contacts. They also should not use automated collection-style calls when there is no overdue balance. More generally, it should be illegal to harass consumers through workplace or automated contacts when they have no delinquent debt.

I use a Senior mobile plan that charges for every text sent or received. If a collector or marketer texts me, I pay even though I did not start the contact. Repeated messages can raise my bill simply because a company chose to contact me. It is unfair to add those costs to existing obligations. Debt collectors should not use charged texts or calls unless the consumer agrees. Businesses should also avoid promotional texts that impose a fee on the recipient. Both should offer a no-cost way to communicate. This would allow legitimate collection or notices without making consumers pay for unwanted contacts.

Policymakers and debt collectors should review the existing bankruptcy documentation framework before adding new validation-notice requirements. Federal Bankruptcy Rule 3001, effective December 1, 2012, together with the published proposal commentary and hearing presentations, provides a relevant reference point for this issue. The Rule already addresses documentation concerns surrounding claims. In my view, requiring every piece of suggested account and ownership documentation to accompany an initial validation notice would not benefit either consumers or issuers. Sending a large packet at the outset can make the important information harder for a consumer to identify and understand. Instead, collectors should provide the core information needed to identify and validate the debt while keeping additional ownership records available when they become necessary. If a collector later files a lawsuit, however, the consumer should be entitled to obtain fuller documentation showing the chain of title before having to defend the case in court. Litigation raises the stakes because the collector is then asking a court to enforce the debt against the consumer. This approach would preserve meaningful access to documentation when it matters most without burdening every routine validation notice with unnecessary material.

Every collection call and dunning notice, whether sent by mail or email, should carry a distinct Collection ID that stays with the account. The same identifier should appear in credit reports so consumers and regulators can connect a reported debt with the collection activity behind it. A stable ID would reduce confusion when several notices or calls concern the same obligation. Consumers should also be able to enter that ID and describe the nature of a suspected violation or problem in an online database managed by the CRPB. This would tie each complaint to a specific collection record. It would also make it easier for the CRPB to compare disputes involving the same ID and determine whether a legitimate issue exists.

When our client cannot verify a disputed debt, we close the collection account and send the debtor a letter confirming the closure. In twenty years, I have seen this happen only once or twice. Such failures have been rare. An unresolved account should not be sold or transferred to another collector. A transfer can force the consumer to dispute the same unverified debt again. The seller should bear responsibility if it transfers such an account. The seller should verify the debt or resolve the dispute before any sale. That rule would prevent an unsupported claim from simply reappearing with a new collector.

Emails from businesses or debt collection agencies should include the sender's state of registration and registration number so consumers can verify who is contacting them. Fraudulent emails are so common that a collection message can be difficult to trust as genuine. Consumers should not have to rely only on links or phone numbers inside a suspicious message to check the sender. Registration details would give recipients information they can verify independently before responding.

Some attorneys identify themselves as 'Debt Collectors' but are not treated as 'Collection Agencies' for oversight or liability. That distinction can leave consumers without a clear way to enforce state or federal consumer-protection requirements. This loophole should be closed so attorney-debt collectors cannot avoid accountability because they operate through a law office. These firms can purchase aged debts and then sue alleged debtors in civil court. Their collection work may fall outside state-bar scrutiny, while civil courts may view the offices as legal practices rather than collection agencies. The result is a regulatory gap in which collection activity can escape oversight. Attorneys who buy debts and litigate them should face the same consumer-protection duties as other debt collectors. State bars and civil courts should have clear authority to address misconduct arising from that activity. A lawyer should not avoid collection rules simply by turning collection into a lawsuit. I am aware of an attorney collection office in Washington State that has conducted classes for other attorneys on this kind of litigation. Those classes have been offered through the Washington State Bar. I understand these cases to be considered comparatively easy to win. That makes oversight more important because the same practices can affect many alleged debtors. Consumers should be able to raise violations against attorney-debt collectors whether the office is labeled a law practice or a collection agency.

Living in Florida, I have become concerned that debt purchasers may rely on altered records to prove collection claims. In my legal case, I received a debt bill of sale with three sections visibly whited out. A lawyer registered with the Florida Bar submitted that altered document. This makes the buyer's claimed ownership difficult to trust. Debt buyers should have to provide complete, unaltered transfer records before collecting. Courts should reject a claim when ownership cannot be shown through authentic documents. Lawyers who submit altered collection records should face professional review because using modified evidence against a consumer lacks basic ethical standards.

The way courts treat consumer default needs reform. The 2013 Compliance issue reinforced my concern that a default is often treated without enough attention to why it happened. Courts should distinguish strategic default from involuntary default when a consumer can document a major life change that made payment temporarily impossible. A borrower who deliberately chooses not to pay is not in the same position as someone whose finances collapse unexpectedly. Qualifying involuntary defaulters should receive relief from continuing interest while their circumstances are reviewed. Otherwise, the balance can keep increasing even when nonpayment was beyond the consumer's control. For several years I have studied consumer debt, and I have become increasingly concerned about its growth around the world. A Canadian financial analyst has warned about rising consumer debt. **URL** Similar concerns extend beyond Canada to England, Australia, South Africa, China, Russia, Ireland, and other countries. One contributor is the very low minimum payment permitted on some credit-card balances, sometimes around 2% per month. A payment set that low can keep borrowers carrying balances while making the debt appear manageable. The problem becomes worse when a major life change produces default and the borrower cannot ask a court to recognize that the default was involuntary. Courts should permit consumers to raise documented involuntary default as a mitigating circumstance in credit-card and student-loan disputes. Consumer-debt cases should not automatically ignore the circumstances behind nonpayment. A fair rule would still require repayment of legitimate principal while giving involuntary defaulters a realistic path to recover instead of allowing interest to grow indefinitely.

I work as the civil clerk at our city court and regularly see consumer-debt cases from filing through judgment. From that position, I believe debtors face significant injustice under the current collection laws. Court staff are not permitted to give legal advice, even when a self-represented defendant does not understand what will happen next. About 95% of the defendants in these cases in my city appear without private counsel. Many fail to answer a summons because service was improper, they ignored it, or, more often in my experience, they do not understand the legal terminology. I frequently receive calls from people asking what they should do after they have been served. When defendants try to answer, I often see informal letters rather than the verified response the procedure expects. Collection attorneys can then move for summary judgment based on the inadequacy of that response. That result is troubling when the consumer tried to participate but did not know the proper form. Pro se defendants who cannot afford counsel should have additional practical ways to respond without receiving individualized legal advice from court staff. Courts should provide a plain-language answer form that identifies the basic issues a defendant may admit, deny, or dispute. Such a form would help distinguish true nonresponse from a good-faith attempt to contest the debt. Our court does not reject informal letters; we send them to the attorney and schedule a pre-trial conference with a judge or court attorney to seek a resolution. We must follow a timetable for those conferences, but when a defendant has a scheduling problem, we try to adjust the date when possible. The summonses themselves vary greatly in the information they provide. Roughly half contain substantial details about the debt, while others state little more than the amount allegedly owed. Every debt-collection complaint should identify the original creditor, the amount claimed, and the basis for added interest or costs. Giving those details at the outset would help a defendant recognize the account and determine what is actually disputed. I also see litigants struggle to obtain documents from collection attorneys even after the court has ordered production. Without those records, it is harder to test whether the plaintiff owns the debt or calculated the balance correctly. Courts should require essential ownership and balance documents before summary judgment or default judgment is entered. When I process a proposed default judgment, I review the file and compare the summons and complaint with the judgment submitted. I check the affidavit of service to make sure the defendant had enough time to respond. I also look for required documentation such as proof of the debt purchase and a non-military affidavit. I separately verify the interest rate and the court costs being charged. These checks matter because a default judgment can be entered without the defendant presenting a full defense. A clearer response procedure and earlier document disclosure would reduce the chance that a valid defense is lost simply because a consumer did not understand court procedure. Ultimately, debtors need stronger procedural protection, while courts need rules that provide it without turning court staff into advocates. The court must remain neutral, and current law limits how much we can do for an unrepresented person. In a small community where many people know one another, it is difficult to watch consumers lose cases for procedural reasons that clearer forms and fuller documentation could prevent.

A debt collector once mailed collection notices to my workplace even though it already had my residential address. Workplace debt mail can expose a private financial problem to coworkers or staff who handle incoming correspondence. That creates needless embarrassment and privacy concerns. When a valid home address is available, using an employer's address is unnecessary. Debt collectors should therefore be barred from mailing notices to a consumer's workplace in that situation. They should use the residential address instead.

I do not answer calls from unknown, anonymous, or toll-free numbers because I cannot tell who is trying to reach me. After more than a year without a job and with only part-time work, I had to give up my landline. My cell phone is now the main number employers can use to contact me. Keeping it active is becoming difficult for me financially. I still receive anonymous calls on that phone even though I notified all creditors in writing not to use my cell number. Creditors and debt collectors should respect a written request not to call a consumer's cell phone. They should use another permitted method of contact instead. Repeated calls can add costs that make it harder for me to keep the phone connected. Losing the phone would also make it harder for an employer to reach me about full-time work. That would work against repayment because steady employment is what would allow me to pay these debts. Once I obtain a full-time job, I want to settle what I owe. The companies making these calls did not extend the credit to me. They should not add cell-phone costs while trying to collect it. Most of the calls I receive are automated and leave no message. When no message is left, I cannot determine whether the call was even intended for me. Collection calls to a cell phone should identify the caller and intended recipient. Anonymous automated calls that leave no message do not give me enough information to know who is calling.

I've carried debt for over 20 years. Several times, I've refinanced and paid everything shown on my credit report. Yet other debts do not surface until it is too late. About once a year, a collector gets a judgment against me and freezes my bank account, causing me to fall behind on bills. Consumers should receive notice before an old debt reaches judgment or an account freeze. The notice should identify the debt and allow time to verify or dispute it. If I clear everything I can see, a hidden claim should not first appear as a frozen account.

Alternative 1 may look like the simplest way to itemize a debt, but its use of the term "principal" hides ambiguity. On revolving credit accounts, interest is added as finance charges and becomes part of the running balance. If principal means only purchases originally made by the cardholder, a later collector may have difficulty reconstructing that figure. If principal instead means the entire charge-off balance, the number may already include substantial interest and fees. Because those definitions can produce very different starting amounts, Alternative 1 is not reliable for a significant share of consumer debt. Alternative 2 has a similar weakness because the point at which an account is considered "defaulted" is not always obvious. A consumer can miss a payment and later bring the account current rather than remain in default. Without a uniform event fixing the default date, creditors could select different balances for similar accounts. These ambiguities make Alternative 3 the most workable approach. Even Alternative 3 needs a rule for accounts for which no periodic or billing statement was provided. When a statement exists, the collection notice should state the amount owed on the last statement sent by the original creditor. That gives the consumer a concrete historical balance tied to an account document. If no statement was ever issued, the notice should begin with the initial amount of the debt. It should then itemize every debit and credit applied after that amount. The itemization should separately identify finance charges, fees, payments, credits, and other adjustments. Showing each later change would let the consumer trace how the collector reached the current total and identify a disputed charge. Without that breakdown, a consumer cannot tell whether an increase came from interest, a fee, or another adjustment. This approach should replace attempts to reconstruct an uncertain original principal or choose an equally uncertain default date.

Debt collectors should be prohibited from repeatedly calling a debtor's former spouse to reach the debtor. Using an ex-spouse as a continuing contact point unfairly pressures someone who does not owe the debt. Collectors sometimes keep using a debtor's old phone number even after it is used solely by the former spouse. Here, the former spouse asks that her number be removed, yet collectors continue calling her to locate the debtor. Collectors should be required to remove a former spouse's number after the first clear request and stop contacting that person about the debt. That request gives the collector notice that the number is no longer an appropriate way to reach the debtor. Continuing to call after that notice turns an attempted contact into avoidable harassment. Without a removal rule, the former spouse has no practical way to make the unwanted calls stop.

MLegz13 has made several persuasive points about debt collection. My aging parents needed help with their daily routines, although they were too proud to admit how much assistance they needed. I put my award-winning video business on hold so I could become their caregiver. I used my savings to cover expenses while I was caring for them, and when those savings ran out, I was facing default even though I had maintained a flawless credit card payment record for 15 years. I did not deny that I owed the debt; I was temporarily without income and unable to keep paying on the old schedule. Even so, collectors kept calling and repeatedly treated me as if I were simply refusing to pay. A consumer in that position should be allowed to stop the debt from escalating at default by formally acknowledging the balance and committing to a repayment plan, even if the first payments are small. A modest payment can demonstrate an intention to resolve the debt while giving someone time to rebuild income. Once that commitment is in place, repeated collection calls should pause while the debtor follows the agreed plan. Constant calls consume time and communication capacity that could instead be used to find work, care for family, and restore finances. My own experience convinced me that this kind of breathing room would make repayment more realistic, not less. That is why I created the Debt Neutrality Petition. More than 500 people have endorsed the petition and left comments about debt collection. One person who identified as a debt collector also endorsed it. Those responses suggest that concern about relentless collection pressure is not limited to debtors alone. I encourage readers to review the petition and its comments rather than dismissing these situations as simple refusal to pay. Debt Neutrality Petition. **URL**

Only the phone number should be visible on caller ID when a debt collector calls. This gives consumers something concrete to check before deciding whether to answer or return the call. Consumers can search the displayed number online to identify the caller. That can also help them recognize repeated collection activity. The number should remain stable enough to identify the collector. A consistent number helps lawyers pursue FDCPA claims because the caller's identity can be tied to the contact.

Consumers should receive clear notice before a delinquent debt is sent to a collection agency. Advance warning gives them time to check the balance or dispute an error before collection begins. If the account later moves to another collector, the consumer should also be told promptly who is handling it. Changing collectors can also change the company name or payment instructions. Notice of that change helps consumers avoid confusion or paying the wrong party.

A debtor should be informed whenever a third party proposes to settle a debt on the debtor's behalf. That notice lets the borrower verify that the proposed settlement is legitimate and matches what is owed. Anyone who pays a debt for another person should disclose their identity to both the lender and the borrower. Knowing who acted gives both sides a clearer record of the settlement and helps the borrower challenge an unfamiliar payment.

Could a national database be established so consumers can report harassing debt-collection calls, especially calls made with disguised or falsified caller ID information? Such a database would help show repeated wrong-number collection activity instead of leaving each person to handle it alone. Several years ago, I obtained a new mobile phone number. Since then, I have received debt-collection calls almost every day from agencies looking for the person who apparently used this number before me. That pattern makes me believe the number was previously assigned to someone who defaulted on financial obligations. I have repeatedly told the callers that they have reached the wrong person and that I do not owe the debt they are trying to collect. Even after those explanations, the calls continue, often from a different displayed number. Many of those numbers appear to be disguised or falsified instead of stable numbers I can identify. That makes ordinary call blocking ineffective because another number can appear on the next call. The calls are also being placed to my mobile phone. I understand there are legal restrictions on collectors repeatedly contacting a cell phone after being told they have the wrong person. I have recorded examples shown on my phone, including 808-792-8186, 858-568-7632, 805-322-4584, 706-913-1192, 808-348-0083, 908-505-9008, 800-633-2677, 571-522-0386, and 858-240-4079. The database should let consumers record the date, displayed number, collector's name when known, and whether the caller has already been told the debt belongs to someone else. Collecting those details would make recurring spoofing and wrong-number harassment easier to investigate.

Individuals can lose their jobs for making or receiving personal calls during work hours. In my previous job, our phone conversations were recorded and occasionally reviewed. I saw employees dismissed without further discussion after they made or accepted personal calls. That experience showed me that an unwanted financial call can put a worker's livelihood at risk. Debt collectors and other financial companies should keep personal matters out of the workplace when another contact method is available. A consumer should be able to provide a personal number or a suitable time for contact instead.

Having worked as a banker in a small institution, I have experienced both sides of debt recovery. Bankers should substantiate a debt and give consumers a real chance to challenge its legitimacy. That lets a person verify the amount before being pressured to pay. Collection agencies contacted our institution about medical debts. I often found their conduct unscrupulous. In several cases, collectors could not explain how the balance was calculated or whether the amount was accurate. I was told the agency could keep about half of what it recovered. That incentive can encourage collection without enough attention to whether every charge is valid. I have seen collectors keep calling even after being asked to stop telephone contact. Repeated calls without a clear accounting pressure consumers without resolving whether the debt is correct. Collection agencies should therefore be prohibited from making collection calls, with substantive communication conducted in writing. Written communication creates a record the consumer can review and dispute. A collection notice should identify the creditor, amount claimed, basis for the balance, and a way to challenge errors. If someone can clearly explain what I owe and why, I am willing to settle a legitimate debt. In the cases I dealt with, collectors did not provide that explanation. Their conduct suggested indifference to whether the balance was correct.

Debt collectors are obligated to identify the creditor to whom the debt is owed when they send a Validation Notice. In my view, that notice is adequate notification that an account has been assigned for collection. A separate notice should still be provided when the debt itself is sold to a new owner. A change in ownership affects whom the consumer owes. That differs from a creditor retaining ownership and hiring an agency or law firm to collect the account. In that situation, I do not think advance notice is necessary before the collector takes the account. The collector's Validation Notice can identify the creditor and tell the consumer who is handling collection. That timing avoids giving the consumer information that may never become true. An agency or law firm can decline an account because of a conflict or another reason. If the creditor had already named that firm, the earlier notice could become inaccurate and create confusion. This approach keeps consumers informed when ownership changes without creating a second notice for a tentative collection referral.

I am worried that there could be a reward system that pays people for reporting that a consumer appears to have a troubled credit situation. Such a system could encourage reports based on incomplete or questionable information. Credit-risk information can affect the price and terms of borrowing. If paid reports make a consumer look riskier, that can lead to increased loan expenses. That possibility sounds like a conspiracy theory to me, but any such reward arrangement should be disclosed so consumers can review what was reported about them.
